title.en: Missing context, wrong context, stale context, conflicting context

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to identify and differentiate missing, wrong, stale, and conflicting context in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems
- 2) Signals, diagnostics, and evaluation metrics to detect each failure mode
- 3) Practical mitigation strategies including indexing, retrieval, reranking, recency controls, authority weighting, and contradiction handling

blocks.title: RAG Tutorial 2025: Complete Introduction to Retrieval Augmented Generation
blocks.label: Course Video

objectiveBefore.fr: Pendant cette vidéo, repérez les éléments qui illustrent « What You Will Learn » avant de poursuivre.
objectiveBefore.en: While watching, identify the elements that illustrate “What You Will Learn” before continuing.

body.en:
RAG systems rely on high-quality retrieval to ground model outputs. Four common failure modes degrade answer quality:

• Missing context (low recall): The retriever fails to fetch relevant evidence. Causes include sparse indexing, poor query formulation, inadequate chunking, or tight top-k cutoffs. Diagnostics: low Recall@k, low MRR, minimal lexical/semantic overlap with gold evidence, high answer abstentions. Mitigations: hybrid BM25+dense retrieval, multi-query expansion, larger k with reranking, better chunking (overlap, windowed), coverage tests against gold corpora.

• Wrong context (low precision): The retriever returns topically similar but irrelevant passages (spurious correlations, overly short chunks, lexical traps). Diagnostics: high rank of distractors, high cross-encoder irrelevance score, error spikes on ambiguous queries. Mitigations: cross-encoder reranking, hard-negative mining, query rewriting/disambiguation, field-scoped search and filters, passage length/section constraints.

• Stale context (out-of-date): Retrieved passages are outdated relative to the question time. Diagnostics: timestamps older than freshness SLA, answers contradict recent updates, recency-weighted precision drops. Mitigations: time-aware ranking (BM25+time decay), TTL and re-embedding policies, streaming/append-only indexes, source-of-truth pinning for latest versions, cache invalidation on updates.

• Conflicting context (contradictions): Retrieved passages disagree (duplicates with drift, multiple authorities). Diagnostics: NLI-based contradiction detection among retrieved passages, source/version divergence, inconsistent numeric values. Mitigations: authority/recency weighting, version canonicalization, de-duplication and document clustering, consensus aggregation (majority/median), explicit citation with per-claim provenance and tie-breaking rules.

Evaluating these modes requires targeted test sets: recall stress tests (multi-hop, paraphrases), distractor-rich precision tests, temporal change sets, and contradiction suites. Instrumentation includes Recall@k, Precision@k, nDCG, MRR, recency-weighted metrics, contradiction rate among top-k, and answer groundedness with per-citation checks.

• Missing context: Recall failure where relevant evidence is not retrieved; improve with hybrid retrieval, larger k + reranking, and query expansion
• Wrong context: Precision failure returning on-topic but irrelevant passages; improve with hard-negative training and cross-encoder reranking
• Stale context: Outdated evidence dominates; mitigate with time-aware scoring, TTL, and authoritative latest-version pinning

• Missing, wrong, stale, and conflicting context are distinct retrieval failures that require targeted diagnostics
• Use hybrid retrieval, reranking, and query rewriting to boost recall and precision
• Enforce freshness, authority, and contradiction resolution to ensure reliable, grounded answers

In this lesson you will learn: 1) A practical taxonomy of hallucinations that appear even in grounded (RAG) systems 2) How to evaluate faithfulness and attribution with automated and human-in-the-loop methods 3) Techniques to reduce hallucinations through prompts, decoding constraints, retrieval design, and verification

Hallucinations in grounded systems occur when outputs are unsupported or contradicted by retrieved evidence. A useful taxonomy includes:

• Attribution hallucination: The model cites sources but the specific claim is not supported by those sources (low attribution precision). Often caused by loose summarization or mixing multiple passages.

• Fabrication under uncertainty: The model invents facts when evidence is missing/ambiguous instead of abstaining (linked to missing context or weak refusal policies).

• Compression/distortion hallucination: During summarization, essential qualifiers (dates, scope, caveats) are dropped, shifting meaning while staying seemingly faithful.

• Entity/temporal conflation: Merging attributes of similar entities or time frames (e.g., versions, years) leading to wrong attributions.

• Numerical/arithmetic hallucination: Incorrect calculations or unit conversions despite available data.

• Contradiction hallucination: Stating a claim that conflicts with retrieved evidence due to poor evidence selection or aggregation.

Evaluation focuses on faithfulness and grounding: answer-supported-by-evidence (ASB) rates, attribution precision/recall, citation coverage, contradiction rate, and span-level entailment checks. Methods include LLM-as-judge with evidence highlighting, NLI models (entail/neutral/contradict), question-answer generation (QAG) consistency, and human spot-checks with provenance. Robust test design uses unanswerable queries, distractor-rich contexts, and contrast sets.

Mitigation strategies: evidence-first plans (select, then generate), cite-then-summarize prompts, constrained decoding (quotes from sources), extraction-before-synthesis pipelines, calculators for numbers, entity normalization, abstain triggers (calibrated uncertainty), and post-generation verifiers that check each claim against evidence and require explicit citations.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to distinguish retrieval failures (missing, noisy, stale, or mis-ranked evidence) from generation failures (hallucination, poor grounding, bad aggregation, or instruction-following errors).
- 2) Practical signals and tests to localize faults, including oracle-context tests, coverage@k, and citation checks.
- 3) A step-by-step diagnosis workflow and targeted remediations for each failure type.

A RAG system has two main stages: retrieval (find and rank evidence) and generation (compose an answer grounded in that evidence). Distinguishing which stage failed is essential for effective fixes.

Retrieval failures: (a) Recall gaps — relevant documents not retrieved due to weak queries, poor embeddings, missing synonyms, or over-tight filters. (b) Precision/noise — many irrelevant chunks crowd out good ones due to loose filters, overly small chunks, or bad reranking. (c) Freshness/index issues — outdated or unindexed content. (d) Chunking/metadata — chunks too small/large, no overlap, missing titles or section tags; poor document IDs.

Generation failures: (a) Hallucination — model states facts absent from context. (b) Misaggregation — merges conflicting passages incorrectly, wrong arithmetic, or chronology errors. (c) Grounding/attribution errors — correct fact but wrong or missing citation. (d) Instruction-following — ignores constraints (format, scope, refusal policy). Causes include prompts that over-prioritize fluency, high temperature, or excessive/unstructured context.

Diagnosis workflow: 1) Reproduce the query with logs: retrieved IDs, scores, chunk texts, and the final prompt. 2) Coverage check: does any retrieved item contain the gold evidence? Compute hit rate/recall@k. Low coverage implies retrieval failure. 3) Oracle-context test: supply the correct passages directly. If the model still errs, the fault is in generation; if it succeeds, the fault is in retrieval/ranking. 4) Ablations: (a) Empty-context run to see closed-book hallucination tendency. (b) Reranker only vs retriever only to isolate ranking issues. 5) Signals: answer mentions entities absent from context, contradictory citations, very low lexical/semantic overlap with retrieved passages, or citations clustered after unsupported claims indicate generation problems; relevant passages appearing beyond top-k or missing key terms indicate retrieval shortcomings.

Remediation: Retrieval — improve query rewriting, add hybrid (BM25 + dense) retrieval, tune top-k and max tokens per doc, increase chunk overlap, enrich metadata, refresh the index, or add domain-specific synonyms. Generation — constrain to cite-then-summarize patterns, require passage IDs per claim, reduce temperature, add reasoning scaffolds for aggregation, and use groundedness/citation validators post hoc.

• Retrieval coverage: Measure hit rate/recall@k against gold passages to detect missing evidence.
• Oracle-context test: Give the model the correct passages; errors then indicate generation issues.
• Precision vs recall tuning: Balance top-k, reranking, chunk size/overlap, and hybrid retrieval to reduce noise while capturing required evidence.

• Use coverage@k and oracle-context tests to separate retrieval from generation errors.
• Retrieval fixes target recall, precision, freshness, and chunking; generation fixes target grounding, aggregation, and instruction-following.
• Log IDs, scores, and citations to make failures auditable and reproducible.
Congratulations! You can now diagnose whether RAG errors arise from retrieval or generation and apply targeted fixes based on clear signals and tests.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to write precise, minimal golden answers that are unambiguous and testable. 2) How to define expected citations (doc IDs, sections, or spans) and evaluate grounding rigorously. 3) How to score content and citations separately to detect unsupported claims and missing evidence.

Golden answers are canonical, concise references used to judge model outputs. They should include only necessary facts, normalize units and names, and avoid stylistic fluff so that matching is deterministic. When multiple phrasings are acceptable, represent them as a set of valid variants (string set, regex, or semantic equivalence rules) rather than a verbose paragraph.

Expected citations specify which sources can support each golden fact. They can be defined at different granularities: document-level (doc ID or canonical URL), section-level (headers/anchors), or span-level (character/token offsets). For many enterprise RAG systems, span- or section-level is preferred to avoid crediting entire documents for unsupported claims. Accept lists can allow multiple valid sources for the same fact.

Evaluation design: (a) Content scoring — exact match, fuzzy/normalized match, or semantic similarity with guardrails (e.g., unit normalization and tolerant date formats). (b) Citation scoring — verify that the output cites at least one acceptable source for each atomic claim; compute citation precision/recall or claim coverage. (c) Coupling — report separate content and citation scores, plus a groundedness flag (content correct AND properly supported). Penalize extra unsupported claims even if the main fact is correct.

Implementation tips: normalize URLs and IDs, version the corpus, snapshot timestamps, and store golds with source IDs to prevent drift. Avoid answer leakage by not putting full gold text verbatim into prompts during evaluation. Build a claim-level schema to map answer segments to required citations. Common pitfalls include overly long gold answers, ambiguous wording, stale golds after document updates, and accepting open-web sources when only curated repositories are allowed.

• Golden answer: Minimal, unambiguous canonical response with normalized entities and units; may include multiple valid variants.
• Expected citations: Enumerated acceptable doc IDs/sections/spans for each fact; match can be strict or soft depending on policy.
• Scoring split: Evaluate content correctness and citation grounding separately; require both for a fully grounded pass.

• Golden answers must be concise, normalized, and unambiguous, with variants encoded explicitly.
• Expected citations define acceptable sources at doc/section/span level and should support claim-by-claim checks.
• Report separate content and citation scores; only answers that are both correct and supported are fully grounded.

Query rewriting transforms the original user input into a form that better matches the corpus and retriever. Techniques include normalization (spelling, casing, lemmatization), canonicalization (expanding acronyms and aliases), disambiguation (adding entity, time, or location qualifiers), paraphrasing to bridge lexical gaps for dense retrievers, and context incorporation from the conversation or task. Effective rewriting improves precision without over-constraining recall.

Question decomposition breaks multi-hop or compound questions into sub-queries that can be answered independently, then aggregated. Common patterns: conjunctive decomposition (A and B), relational/hop-based (entity -> relation -> attribute), temporal decomposition (then vs now), and constraint extraction (topic, facet, filter). Execution plans include sequential retrieval with working memory, tree-based decomposition, and iterative refinement using LLMs to generate and verify sub-questions. Pitfalls include error propagation, answer aggregation conflicts, and excessive latency; mitigations include re-ranking, caching partial results, and limiting fan-out.

HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) prompts an LLM to draft a short, plausible answer-like passage for the query. You embed that synthetic passage and retrieve real documents by similarity, optionally re-ranking with a cross-encoder. HyDE improves recall when the query is short, under-specified, or uses vocabulary that differs from the corpus. Risks: anchoring to hallucinated details, topic drift, and added cost/latency. Mitigations: keep the hypothetical passage concise, avoid fabricated named entities, constrain style to neutral summaries, and always validate with retrieved sources.

• Query rewriting: Normalize, disambiguate, and paraphrase to align the query with corpus language and retriever behavior.
• Question decomposition: Split complex intents into executable sub-queries; sequence retrieval and aggregate answers carefully.
• HyDE: Generate a hypothetical passage to embed for retrieval, boosting recall while guarding against hallucination anchoring.

• Query rewriting improves alignment with the corpus and reduces ambiguity.
• Decomposition turns multi-hop questions into tractable steps with better evidence quality.
• HyDE can raise recall in sparse or lexically mismatched settings but must be constrained to avoid anchoring errors.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to generate and manage multiple query variants to boost recall and reduce false negatives. 2) How to retrieve across multiple indexes (BM25, dense, code, tables, multimodal) and fuse results effectively. 3) How to route queries, deduplicate, re-rank, and balance quality with cost and latency.

Multi-query retrieval issues diverse paraphrases or facet-focused variants to cover different lexical/semantic angles. Generation strategies include synonym/phrase expansions, step-back generalizations (ask for the principle, then specifics), entity/alias injection, and constraint-focused variants (time, locale, version). Control fan-out using diversity selection (e.g., MMR on embeddings), ceilings on variants, and early stopping when marginal recall plateaus.

Result fusion combines hits from each variant. Robust methods include Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which is rank-based and avoids score normalization, and weighted fusion with min–max or z-score normalization plus learned weights. After fusion, deduplicate by stable doc IDs and re-rank with a cross-encoder or LLM-as-a-reranker. Guardrails: cap per-variant top_k, shard-parallelize, and cache frequent variants.

Multi-index retrieval queries different indexes specialized by signal or modality: BM25 for exact terms, dense vectors for semantics, code/AST indexes for programming queries, table/SQL for structured facts, and image/audio embeddings for multimodal RAG. Routing options include: always-on fusion (query all), learned routing (classifier chooses indexes), or rules (e.g., presence of code fences -> code index). Normalize scores before weighted fusion across heterogeneous indexes or prefer RRF. Evaluate with recall@k, MRR, nDCG, diversity metrics, and end-task quality; track cost and p95 latency. Typical pitfalls: topic drift from too many variants, double-counting near-duplicates, and unnecessary index fan-out increasing cost.

Agentic RAG turns the LLM into a planner that decides what to retrieve, from where, and in which order. A typical loop is Plan → Retrieve → Read → Reason → Verify → Stop.

The planner decomposes complex questions into sub-goals, selects tools or sources (vector store, keyword search, web, SQL, code), formulates/reforms queries, and sets budgets (k per hop, maximum hops, token caps). Adaptive strategies route sub-questions to the best source (e.g., code Q&A to a docs index, current events to web) and adjust k based on uncertainty.

Stopping criteria include confidence thresholds (e.g., entailment score from evidence), self-consistency across sampled answers, or lack-of-progress signals. Verification adds robustness via evidence checking (citation coverage), cross-checking with alternative queries, or answerability detection that returns “not enough information.” Logging traces of actions, queries, and evidence enables step-level evaluation (sub-answer accuracy, evidence recall/precision) and cost control (per-hop tokens, API calls).

• Source routing and tool use: Choose the right index or external tool for each sub-goal and reformulate queries as needed.
• Verification and stopping: Use confidence signals, entailment/citation checks, and early stopping to control cost and improve reliability.

title.en: Synthetic Dataset Generation for RAG Evaluation

body.en:
Evaluating a RAG system requires ground-truth data: questions paired with relevant contexts and reference answers. In production, such datasets are expensive and slow to create manually. Synthetic generation solves this by prompting an LLM to produce question-answer pairs directly from your document corpus.

The standard pipeline involves three steps. First, chunk your documents into passages. Second, prompt a capable LLM (e.g., GPT-4 or Claude) to generate one or more questions that are answerable from each passage, along with a reference answer grounded in that passage. Third, optionally introduce distractor passages to simulate hard negatives.

Key considerations include controlling question type diversity (factoid, multi-hop, abstractive), tuning difficulty, and filtering low-quality samples using a secondary LLM judge or heuristics such as answer length and overlap with the source. Tools like RAGAS, Giskard, and LlamaIndex Evaluation support automated synthetic dataset creation, offering configurable templates and quality checks. Always hold out a manually curated sample to audit synthetic data quality before trusting evaluation scores derived from it.

title.en: Retrieval Metrics: Recall, Precision, MRR, nDCG

body.en:
Retrieval quality determines the ceiling of any RAG system. If the retriever fails to surface relevant passages, even the best generator cannot produce accurate answers. Quantifying retrieval quality requires metrics that account for both relevance and rank.

Recall@K measures the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved within the top-K results. It answers: 'Did we find everything we needed?' Precision@K measures the fraction of top-K retrieved documents that are actually relevant, answering: 'How much of what we returned was useful?' There is an inherent tension between these two metrics.

Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) focuses on the rank of the first relevant document. For each query, the reciprocal rank is 1/rank_of_first_relevant; MRR is the mean across all queries. It is ideal when users only care about the top result.

nDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) is the most expressive metric. It handles graded relevance (e.g., highly relevant, partially relevant, not relevant) and discounts the gain of relevant documents found at lower ranks using a logarithmic penalty. DCG is normalized by the ideal DCG (IDCG) to produce a score between 0 and 1 that is comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant documents. Retrieval quality determines the ceiling of any RAG system. If the retriever fails to surface relevant passages, even the best generator cannot produce accurate answers. Quantifying retrieval quality requires metrics that account for both relevance and rank.

Recall@K measures the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved within the top-K results. It answers: 'Did we find everything we needed?' Precision@K measures the fraction of top-K retrieved documents that are actually relevant, answering: 'How much of what we returned was useful?' There is an inherent tension between these two metrics.

Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) focuses on the rank of the first relevant document. For each query, the reciprocal rank is 1/rank_of_first_relevant; MRR is the mean across all queries. It is ideal when users only care about the top result.

nDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) is the most expressive metric. It handles graded relevance (e.g., highly relevant, partially relevant, not relevant) and discounts the gain of relevant documents found at lower ranks using a logarithmic penalty. DCG is normalized by the ideal DCG (IDCG) to produce a score between 0 and 1 that is comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant documents. For RAG, nDCG@K is often the preferred metric because it aligns with the reality that passages vary in how well they answer a question.

Once retrieval is evaluated, you must assess what the LLM generates with the retrieved context. Three dimensions dominate RAG generation evaluation.

Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context. A faithful answer never introduces information beyond what the context provides, even if that information is true. The RAGAS framework operationalizes faithfulness by decomposing the answer into atomic claims and verifying each against the context using an LLM judge. A score of 1.0 means all claims are grounded; 0.0 means none are.

Helpfulness (sometimes called answer relevancy) measures how well the answer actually addresses the user's question. An answer can be perfectly faithful yet still unhelpful if it cites tangentially related context or buries the key information. Helpfulness is typically assessed by an LLM judge that asks whether the response would satisfy the user's intent.

Correctness measures factual accuracy relative to a ground-truth reference answer. Unlike faithfulness, correctness is not restricted to the context; it compares the generated answer to known facts. Metrics include exact match, F1 over tokens, BERTScore for semantic similarity, and LLM-based semantic correctness scoring. In practice, faithfulness and correctness can diverge: a model may faithfully reproduce a wrong passage (high faithfulness, low correctness) or correctly answer from memory while ignoring the context (low faithfulness, high correctness).

As RAG evaluation scales beyond what human annotators can review, practitioners rely on powerful LLMs to score system outputs. An LLM judge receives a question, optionally retrieved context, a generated answer, and a scoring rubric, then outputs a score or preference judgment. Frameworks like RAGAS, MT-Bench, and Prometheus have popularized this approach.

However, LLM judges carry systematic biases. Position bias causes judges to favor answers presented first in pairwise comparisons. Verbosity bias causes judges to prefer longer answers regardless of quality. Self-enhancement bias means a model tends to rate outputs from itself or similar models more favorably. Sycophancy bias causes judges to prefer answers that agree with their own prior outputs or the framing of the prompt.

Calibration is the process of aligning LLM judge scores with human judgment. This involves collecting a human-annotated calibration set, computing correlation coefficients (Cohen's kappa, Spearman rho) between judge scores and human scores, and iterating on judge prompts and rubrics until agreement is acceptable.

Mitigation strategies include: swap augmentation (presenting each answer pair in both orders and averaging scores to cancel position bias), panel judging (using multiple diverse LLMs and aggregating scores), chain-of-thought scoring (requiring the judge to reason step by step before assigning a score), and reference-guided scoring (providing a gold reference answer to anchor the rubric). These techniques together produce judges that are more reliable, consistent, and aligned with human evaluators.

RAG systems change frequently (embeddings, retrievers, chunking, rerankers, prompts, and generators), so layered regression testing is essential. Use unit tests for components (e.g., tokenizer/chunker), integration tests for retrieval pipelines (retriever + reranker), and end-to-end tests for answer quality and groundedness.

Create gold datasets: (a) retrieval sets with queries and expected relevant document IDs, (b) answer sets with references/citations, and (c) adversarial/slice sets (long queries, entities, multi-hop). Track metrics by layer: retrieval (Recall@k, Precision@k, MRR, nDCG), attribution/groundedness (supportedness, citation accuracy), and generation (Exact Match, token F1, ROUGE-L, answerability).

Stabilize tests by pinning versions, snapshotting indexes/embeddings, fixing top_k, setting temperature=0, seeding data order, and caching reranker/model outputs where feasible. Run CI on pull requests with acceptance thresholds and bootstrap-based significance checks, and schedule nightly full suites.

Use slice analysis, cost/latency monitoring, and change logs for traceability. Treat regressions with a triage process and avoid masking problems (e.g., arbitrarily raising k).

• Metrics by layer: Recall@k/MRR for retrieval; groundedness/attribution checks; EM/F1/ROUGE-L for answers; plus latency and cost budgets
• Test stability: Temperature=0, seeded order, fixed top_k, snapshot embeddings/index, version pinning for retrievers/rerankers

• Test by layer and by slice; do not rely on a single end-to-end score

Feedback loops turn user signals and annotations into continuous improvements. Collect explicit signals (thumbs up/down, 5-point ratings, pairwise preferences, suggested fixes), implicit signals (clicks, dwell time, abandonment), and issue reports.

Define a labeling schema for RAG: relevance grades for retrieved docs, answer correctness, groundedness/attribution (is the claim supported by cited passages?), completeness, and safety. Produce thorough guidelines with positive/negative examples and edge cases, and run calibration rounds.

Ensure quality with inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha), hidden gold checks, spot audits, and reviewer workflows. Triage feedback: deduplicate, categorize, prioritize high-impact slices, and protect privacy/PII.

Integrate labels: improve retriever/reranker training data, update prompts, fix indexing/chunking, and add cases to evaluation suites. Use active learning/uncertainty sampling to select items for annotation.

Version datasets and label schemas, and measure loop health (throughput, agreement, time-to-fix, regression reoccurrence). Deploy improvements with feature flags and monitor post-release.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to design reproducible experiment tracking for RAG systems (datasets, prompts, retrievers, indexes, models, and evaluators).
- 2) How to define and automate release gates tied to evaluation thresholds, risk, and business SLAs.
- 3) How to operationalize experiments in CI/CD with canaries, shadowing, approvals, and rollback procedures.

Experiment tracking ensures results are reproducible and comparable across iterations.

Each run should capture immutable metadata: code commit/artefact version, dataset and query set versions, prompt template hash, retriever parameters (e.g., top_k, filters), index snapshot ID, model and tokenizer versions, evaluator versions, random seeds, and environment details.

For RAG, track both offline and online metrics: answer correctness/utility (LLM-graded or human), faithfulness/groundedness, citation accuracy, retrieval precision/recall, latency, cost per query, and safety/PII incidents.

Statistical rigor matters: use fixed test sets, holdouts, and significance testing or Bayesian estimation when comparing variants.

Release gates are policy rules that block promotion unless multi-metric thresholds are satisfied (e.g., faithfulness ≥ 0.9, citation accuracy ≥ 0.95, latency p95 ≤ 800 ms, safety incidents = 0).

Gates can be risk-weighted, applying stricter criteria for high-impact domains.

Progressive delivery reduces risk: shadow traffic validates correctness without user impact; canaries expose a small slice with automatic abort thresholds; A/B tests measure business impact.

Automate gates in CI/CD so a pipeline promotes only when metrics, sample sizes, and checks pass, with human sign-off for exceptions and documented rollback plans.

• Experiment lineage and versioning: Record code, data, prompts, retriever/index snapshots, models, and evaluator versions to ensure exact reproducibility.
• Release gates and policies: Multi-metric, risk-aware thresholds that must be met before promotion, covering quality, latency, cost, and safety.
• Progressive delivery: Shadow, canary, and A/B strategies with automatic aborts and rollbacks to minimize user risk during releases.

• Track full lineage (code, data, prompts, retriever/index, models, evaluators) for reproducible RAG experiments.
• Define multi-metric, risk-aware release gates and automate them in CI/CD.
• Use shadowing/canaries with clear abort and rollback criteria to de-risk releases.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to track RAG experiments rigorously and enforce release gates safely in production.

title.en: Reporting to product and business stakeholders

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to translate RAG evaluation metrics into business impact and risk. 2) How to build stakeholder-ready dashboards and reports that are concise and trustworthy. 3) How to make decision-ready recommendations with clear trade-offs and next steps.

Effective reporting starts with audience alignment.

For product and business leaders, begin with a one-page executive summary: what changed, observed impact, risk, and the decision being requested (go/no-go/iterate).

Tie technical metrics to outcomes: answer acceptance and faithfulness map to ticket deflection and CSAT; latency p95 maps to conversion and satisfaction; cost/query maps to gross margin; safety incidents map to compliance risk.

Present results with uncertainty: include sample sizes, confidence intervals, and known biases (e.g., domain skew).

Segment results by cohorts (intent, channel, locale) to reveal where improvements matter most.

Use simple visuals and consistent definitions (north-star metric, leading indicators, guardrail metrics).

State release readiness against SLAs/SLOs and policy gates, list trade-offs (quality vs. latency vs. cost), and quantify incremental impact (e.g., +4% acceptance → −3% tickets/month).

Close with actionable next steps, owners, and timelines, and link to experiment lineage for auditability.

• North-star metrics and guardrails: Define the primary business outcome and supporting constraints (quality, latency, cost, safety).
• Communicating uncertainty: Report point estimates with confidence intervals and sample sizes to avoid overclaiming.
• Decision-ready storytelling: Lead with impact, risk, and a clear ask; keep methods and lineage available in an appendix.

• Translate technical metrics into business terms (deflection, CSAT, margin) with uncertainty and sample sizes.
• Use consistent, decision-focused reporting: impact, risks, trade-offs, and a clear ask.
• Provide drill-downs and lineage for auditability while keeping the main narrative concise.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now communicate RAG evaluation results clearly to product and business stakeholders and drive informed decisions.
